We grew up side by side, with somewhat less than a year between our ages. It scarcely needs saying that no quarrel or estrangement ever divided us. Concord animated our companionship, while the differences and oppositions in our dispositions served only to bring us closer. Elizabeth's nature was quieter and more collected; yet, ardent as I was, I could devote myself more intensely to a subject and felt a deeper thirst for learning. She occupied herself with the airy inventions of poets. In the grand and marvellous landscape about our Swiss home—the sublime mountain forms, the seasons' changes, storms and stillness, winter's silence, and the stir and vitality of Alpine summers—she discovered inexhaustible sources of wonder and pleasure. While she regarded the splendid outward aspect of things with grave contentment, I took delight in tracing their causes. To me the world was a mystery waiting to be deciphered. Among my first remembered feelings are curiosity, eager efforts to discover nature's secret laws, and a joy approaching ecstasy whenever those laws became clear.

When a second son was born, seven years younger than I, my parents entirely relinquished their wandering existence and settled in their own country. We owned a house in Geneva and a country residence at Belrive, on the eastern bank of the lake, rather more than a league outside the city. We lived chiefly at the latter, where my parents passed their days in considerable retirement. My disposition inclined me to shun crowds and devote myself warmly to a few. Thus I felt little attachment to my schoolmates in general, but formed the closest friendship with one of them. Henry Clerval was a Geneva merchant's son, a boy of uncommon gifts and imagination. He delighted in bold undertakings, hardship, and danger itself. He had read deeply in romances and tales of chivalry, composed heroic verses, and begun many stories of enchantment and knightly exploits. He sought to persuade us to perform plays and take part in masquerades, choosing our characters from the heroes of Roncesvalles, King Arthur's Round Table, and the gallant company who had shed their blood to recover the holy sepulchre from the infidels.

No one could have enjoyed a happier childhood than mine. Kindness and indulgence seemed the very essence of my parents. We never regarded them as tyrants who would dispose of our lives according to their whims, but as the authors and providers of all the pleasures that surrounded us.

But I have dwelt on this enough. I shall begin my story: it is the last duty left to me, and I trust my strength will suffice to complete it. No crimes are recorded here. My errors deserve easy forgiveness, having sprung not from wicked intentions but from defective judgment. Few, I think, could claim that wiser conduct would have enabled them to escape the disasters of which I am the victim. Necessity, a dreadful necessity, has ruled my destiny. To break the massive, adamantine chain that bound me would have required hands stronger than my own—stronger, I believe, than any human power. That chain bound one who once breathed only happiness, whose heart was always warm with love and delight in goodness, to suffering that death alone could end and is now about to end. Yet I forget myself; my history remains untold. I will stop briefly, dry my clouded eyes, and try to lose the dull but weighty unhappiness of the present in the sharper feelings of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of distinguished rank. His father died when he was young, and a weak mother brought him up with every indulgence she believed appropriate to a wealthy nobleman. He went first to Eton and then to college, and from childhood was permitted unrestricted use of large sums. Consequently, he enjoyed from his earliest youth the independence a boy so favoured invariably acquires at a public school.

In these circumstances his passions found fertile earth in which to take root and flourish, as flowers or weeds according to their nature. Always allowed to choose for himself, he developed a strongly marked character early, presenting varied features in which a discerning observer might detect the beginnings both of virtue and of calamity. His heedless extravagance, which squandered immense amounts upon passing fancies he dignified as passions because they seemed so vigorous, frequently showed itself as limitless generosity. Yet even while he earnestly attended to other people's needs, his own desires received complete satisfaction. He gave money without sacrificing any wish of his own. He bestowed time, which he held cheap, and affection, which he was pleased to have awakened by any means.

I do not assert that, had his wishes competed with those of others, he would have proved excessively selfish. But that test was never imposed. Prosperity had nourished him and surrounded him with all its benefits. Everyone loved him, and everyone sought to please him.

I offered my thanks and an apology. “Not at all,” he answered, and went on.

“Miss Havisham had become an heiress and was naturally sought as a magnificent match. Her half-brother again possessed considerable resources, but debts and fresh follies soon caused him to squander them disgracefully. His disagreements with her were fiercer than those he had had with his father, and he is believed to have borne her a deep and deadly resentment, supposing that she had inflamed his father's anger. Now we reach the cruel portion of the history. I interrupt myself only, my dear Handel, to observe that a dinner-napkin cannot be put inside a tumbler.”

I have no possible explanation for my attempt to force my napkin into my glass. I know only that I discovered myself labouring strenuously to compress it into those narrow bounds, with a persistence deserving a far worthier object. Once more I thanked him and begged pardon; once more he replied with perfect good humour, “Not at all, indeed!” and continued.

“A particular man then made his appearance—at the races, let us say, or the public assemblies, or wherever you please—and began paying court to Miss Havisham. I never knew him, since this occurred five-and-twenty years ago, before either you or I existed, Handel. But my father has described him as a showy fellow and just the man for such a purpose. My father insists most strongly, however, that only ignorance or prejudice could have mistaken him for a gentleman. He maintains that, since the beginning of the world, no one who lacked a gentleman's heart ever truly possessed a gentleman's manners. Varnish, he says, cannot conceal wood's grain; the more you apply, the plainer the grain becomes. Well, this fellow pursued Miss Havisham assiduously, declaring complete devotion. I believe she had displayed little tenderness of that sort before, but whatever capacity for it she possessed certainly emerged now. She loved him with passion; indeed, she unquestionably idolized him. By methodically working upon her affection, he extracted large sums. He also induced her to purchase her brother's interest in the brewery at an enormous price—an interest their father had weakly bequeathed him—claiming that upon their marriage he must own and direct the entire concern. Your guardian had not yet become one of Miss Havisham's advisers, and her pride and infatuation were too great to permit her to accept counsel from anybody.
